topics.title: How to learn Lebanese with Kifak
topics.summary: A plan for your first three months, and how to use each part of the site.

blocks.text: Listen first, read second. Lebanese is a spoken language: people rarely write it except in text messages, so your ear matters more than your eyes.
Do a little every day. Fifteen minutes daily beats two hours on Sunday.
Say everything out loud. The **Repeat** step in each lesson records you so you can compare with the native voice.

sections.h: A plan for the first three months

head: Weeks
What to do
Goal
rows: Read 2, 3, 7, kh, gh, sh without thinking. 300 words.
Level 2, the Grammar basics, Review every day
Put two or three words together.
Levels 3 and 4, Verbs, Conversations of Level 1 to 4
Talk about your day and what you did yesterday.

blocks.text: **Lessons:** the main path. Learn the cards, repeat them, then take the quiz. Each quiz picks 15 new examples, so take it more than once.
**Review:** flashcards of words from lessons you finished. Cards you know come back less often; cards you miss come back soon. Do it every day.
**Conversations:** real dialogues. Listen once without reading, then with the text, then answer the questions.
**Verbs:** the tables. Learn the "every day" form first, because the others are built from it.
**Grammar** and **Culture:** read a page when a lesson raises a question.
**Dictionary:** search any word in English, Latin letters or Arabic.
Hide the English with the EN button once a lesson feels easy. Hide the Latin letters too if you're learning the Arabic script.
Lebanese people switch between Arabic, French and English, often in one sentence. You'll hear "merci", "bonjour" and "ok" all day. That's normal Lebanese, not a mistake.
Most Lebanese will answer you in English or French the moment they hear an accent. Smile and keep going in Arabic: "baddi et3allam 3arabe" (I want to learn Arabic). Most people love it.

topics.title: The sounds of Lebanese
topics.summary: The letters English doesn't have, doubled letters, and which syllable to stress.

head: Latin
Arabic
How to say it
Example
rows: A tiny stop in the throat, like the break in "uh-oh".
Squeeze the throat, as if starting to gag, then say "a".
A strong breathy "h", like fogging up glasses.

blocks.text: Four letters have a "heavy" twin, said with the tongue pulled back: ص (s), ض (d), ط (t), ظ (z). Latin-script Arabic writes them like the light ones, so "sayf" and "seif" can look alike. The heavy ones make the vowel near them sound darker, more like "o" or "a" in "father".
You don't need the heavy sounds to be understood at first. Get 3, 7 and 2 right first; people will understand you.
A doubled letter is held longer, and it changes the meaning. Listen carefully to these pairs.

Lebanese has short a, e, i, o, u and long ones. In Latin letters people write "e" for a sound between "e" in "bed" and "a" in "cat". Long vowels are often written double or with "ei" and "ou": "beit" (house), "rou7" (go).
In Beirut many "a" sounds at the end of words become "e": "a7la" in a book is "a7le" in the street. That's the "imala", and it's one of the clearest marks of Lebanese.

blocks.english: How are you doing? (to a woman)

blocks.text: Stress the long vowel if there is one: "sha-BEB" (young men), "ma-TAR" (airport). If there isn't, stress the second-to-last syllable: "MAD-rase" (school). Lebanese is spoken fast, and short vowels often disappear: "ktir", not "katir".

mistakes: Saying "h" for 7 or nothing for 3. "3am" (in the middle of) and "am" don't mean the same thing.
Rushing doubled letters. "7ammam" (bathroom) said with one m is "7amam" (pigeons).

quiz.q: Which number stands for the letter ع?
In "7ammam" (bathroom), what do you do with the m?
Which sound is like the "ch" in Scottish "loch"?

topics.title: I, you, he, she: pronouns
topics.summary: The eight people every verb and every ending is built on.

blocks.text: Lebanese has three ways to say "you": one for a man, one for a woman, one for a group. Every verb changes with them, so learn which one you are using.
English "it" is huwwe or hiyye: every noun is masculine or feminine (see the next topic).
The verb already shows who is talking, so the pronoun is extra. Use it for emphasis or contrast.
Lebanese use "ento" (plural) to be polite to one older person, a bit like French "vous". "kifkon?" to your friend's grandmother sounds warm.

quiz.q: How do you say "you" to a woman?

topics.title: "To be": I am, I was, I'll be
topics.summary: There's no "am / is / are" in the present. You just put the words side by side.

blocks.text: "I'm tired" is simply "I tired". "The house is big" is "the house big".
Put **mesh** before the word: "mesh te3ban" (not tired). Some people say "mish" or "ma-ni" forms ("mani te3ban"); "mesh" works everywhere.
For the past you need a verb: ken (was).
Put ken before an every-day verb (without b-) and you get "used to". Put it before 3am and you get "was doing".

blocks.english: I used to go to the sea every day
I was eating when she came

mistakes: Adding a word for "is": "el beit huwwe kbir" sounds odd. Just "el beit kbir".
Using "ma" in the present: it's "mesh te3ban", not "ma te3ban".

topics.title: Masculine and feminine
topics.summary: Every noun is a he or a she, and the words around it follow.

sections.h: How to spot a feminine word

blocks.text: Most feminine words end in **-e** or **-a** (in Arabic, ة): sayyara (car), madrase (school), tawle (table), shante (bag).
Some are feminine without the ending: words for women (emm: mother), most body parts that come in pairs (iid: hand, 3ein: eye), and some others like ard (ground) and shams (sun).
Adjectives, "this", verbs and endings all change.

sections.h: Talking to a man or a woman

blocks.text: Lebanese also changes words depending on who you talk to. "How are you?" is "kifak?" to a man and "kifik?" to a woman. Use the "Talking to" switch in lessons to see both.
A woman says "ana te3bene", "ana mabsouta", "ana lebnenye". A man says "ana te3ban", "ana mabsout", "ana lebnene". Get this right about yourself first.

mistakes: Using the man's form for yourself if you're a woman (or the other way). People will understand, but it's the mistake they notice most.

topics.title: Plurals and "two of"
topics.summary: -in, -et, the "broken" plurals, and the -ein ending for pairs.

blocks.text: Most words for people and jobs add **-in**: m3allem → m3allmin (teachers), lebnene → lebnenyin (Lebanese people).
Most feminine words swap -e/-a for **-et**: sayyara → sayyarat (cars), tawle → tawlet (tables), shante → shanatet (bags).
Many common words change their inside instead. There's a pattern, but learn them one by one.
Add **-ein** for exactly two: yom → yomein (two days), sene → sentein (two years), kilo → kiloyein. You don't need the number 2.
For plural things (not people), adjectives often take the feminine: "el byout ghalye", "sayyarat jdide". People stay plural: "el shabeb mabsoutin".

mistakes: Saying "tnein yom" for two days. Lebanese say "yomein".

topics.title: "The": el- and the sun letters
topics.summary: One word for "the", and why it sometimes sounds like ech-, et- or es-.

blocks.text: Put **el** (or just **l** after a vowel) in front: beit (a house), el beit (the house). There's no word for "a": beit is "a house".

blocks.english: There's a book on the table

blocks.text: Before t, d, s, sh, z, r, n, l and the heavy letters, the l of "el" melts into the next letter. You write "el shams" but say "esh-shams". The Latin spelling on this site follows what you hear in some places and what you write in others, so listen to the recording.

head: Written
Said
English
rows: not a sun letter: l is said

blocks.text: Lebanese uses "the" more than English: for things in general ("I love coffee" = "b7ebb el ahwe"), for languages, and for names of meals.
"the" plus a preposition usually shrinks: "3a + el beit" → "3al beit" (to the house), "b + el beit" → "bel beit" (at home), "la + el beit" → "lal beit".

topics.title: My, your, his: the endings
topics.summary: Lebanese doesn't say "my book", it says "book-my". Learn the eight endings once and they work everywhere.

blocks.text: A word ending in -e/-a gets a **t** before the ending: sayyara → sayyarte (my car), sayyartak (your car), sayyarta (her car).

These endings also go on prepositions ("ma3e": with me, "3ande": at me = I have) and on verbs as "me, you, him" ("shefto": I saw him, "b7ebbik": I love you, to a woman). Learn them here and you've learned them for the whole language.
You can also say "el kteb taba3e" (the book of mine). It's useful for emphasis and for long or foreign words: "el laptop taba3e" sounds more natural than "laptope".

topics.title: This and that
topics.summary: hayda, hayde, hawde, and the short "hal".

blocks.text: Before a noun, Lebanese often use the short **hal**: "hal beit" (this house), "hal marra" (this time). It's the same for men and women.

topics.title: Describing things, comparing
topics.summary: The adjective goes after the noun. "Bigger" and "the biggest" are one short word.

blocks.note: "the" on the noun only makes a sentence

blocks.text: Most adjectives have a short form for comparing: kbir → akbar (bigger), zghir → azghar, 7elo → a7la, ghali → aghla, rkhis → arkhas, ktir → aktar, mni7 → a7san. Add **men** for "than".
Put the comparative first: "akbar beit" (the biggest house), "a7la wa7ad" (the nicest one).

blocks.english: the best food in the world

blocks.text: Adjectives that don't have a short form use **aktar** (more): "mertee7 aktar" (more comfortable).
ktir = very, a lot (after or before the adjective). shway = a bit. "ktir ktir" = really very.

mistakes: Putting the adjective first: "kbir beit". It's "beit kbir".

topics.title: Numbers in real life
topics.summary: Counting things, big numbers, prices and "first, second".

blocks.text: Before a noun, 3 to 10 lose their ending: tlet (3), arba3 (4), khams (5), set (6), sab3 (7), tmen (8), tes3 (9), 3ashr (10). The noun is plural.
"One" goes after the noun or is just the noun: "kteb" (a book), "kteb wa7ad" (one book). "Two" is the -ein ending: "ktebein".
11 7da3sh, 12 tna3sh, 13 tletta3sh, 14 arba3ta3sh, 15 khamsta3sh, 16 setta3sh, 17 saba3ta3sh, 18 tmenta3sh, 19 tes3ta3sh. From 11 up, the noun goes back to singular: "tna3sh sene" (12 years).
Tens: 20 3eshrin, 30 tletin, 40 arb3in, 50 khamsin, 60 settin, 70 sab3in, 80 tmenin, 90 tes3in. 25 is "khamse w 3eshrin" (five and twenty).
Prices are said with the number first: "3ashr dollar", "khamsin alf". In daily life people often just say the number: "addeish? 3eshrin" (How much? Twenty).
awwal (first), tene (second), telet (third), rabe3 (fourth), akher (last). "awwal marra" = the first time.

mistakes: "tlete byout": before a noun use the short form "tlet byout".
"tna3sh snin": after 10, the noun is singular again, "tna3sh sene".

topics.title: Saying no: ma, mesh, wala
topics.summary: Which "not" goes where, with a cheat sheet.

blocks.english: I never speak / not at all

blocks.text: la2 = no. la2 la2 = no no (firm). "mesh hayk" = not like that. A quick lift of the chin with a click of the tongue ("tsk") also means no.
"ma" and "mesh" are the most common words in any language course; get these two right and half of your "no" sentences are done.

mistakes: "mesh ba3ref": it's "ma ba3ref" (ma before a verb).
"ma mni7": it's "mesh mni7" (mesh before an adjective).

topics.title: Asking questions
topics.summary: The question words, and how a statement turns into a question.

sections.h: Yes/no questions: just raise your voice

blocks.text: "enta lebnene." (You're Lebanese.) → "enta lebnene?" (Are you Lebanese?) Same words, rising voice.

blocks.english: Where are you going? (to a man)

sections.h: The question word goes first or last

blocks.text: Both work: "shu baddak?" and "baddak shu?" (What do you want?). Putting it last sounds more surprised.
"mazbout?" (right?), "aw la2?" (or not?), "sa77?" (correct?) at the end of a sentence check that you understood.

topics.title: There is, there isn't: fi
topics.summary: One tiny word does the work of "there is", "there are", "is there?"

blocks.english: There are a lot of people

blocks.text: "fiye" (with the endings) means "I can". "fi" with no ending in a question can mean "is it possible?". See "Want, can, have to".

blocks.english: Can I do something? / Is there anything I can do?

topics.title: To have: 3ande
topics.summary: Lebanese has no verb "to have". You say "at me there is": 3ande.

blocks.text: "3and" also means "at the house of": "ana 3and teta" (I'm at grandma's). "3enna" (at ours) is how you invite someone: "ta3a la 3enna" (come over to ours).
"I have money (on me)" is "ma3e masari". Use ma3e (with me) for what's in your pocket right now.

blocks.english: Do you have money on you?

topics.title: Want, can, have to
topics.summary: badde, fiye / 2ader, lezim, and the verb that follows them.

blocks.text: badde takes the possessive endings, like 3ande.
After badde, the verb drops its b-: "bekol" (I eat) → "badde ekol" (I want to eat).

blocks.english: What do you want to eat? (to a man)

blocks.text: **fiye** (fiye, fik, fike, fi, fia, fina, fikon, fion) and **2ader** (I'm able; 2adra for a woman) both mean "can". fiye is more common for permission, 2ader for ability.

blocks.english: Can you help me? (to a man)

blocks.text: **lezim** doesn't change. Put the verb (without b-) after it.

blocks.english: You have to try the knafeh
You don't have to / no need

sections.h: Other words that work the same way

blocks.text: ma3 enno (although), 3ashen (so that), 2abel ma (before), ba3d ma (after): all followed by the verb without b-.

mistakes: "badde berou7": after badde, drop the b-: "badde rou7".
Changing lezim: it stays "lezim" for everyone.

topics.summary: The prepositions you'll use in every sentence, with and without endings.

blocks.text: They all take the possessive endings. A few change a little.

blocks.english: This is for you (to a man)
between you and you (just between us)
The house is next to the school

blocks.text: "3leye" is how you insist on paying. Expect a friendly argument: everyone says "la2, 3leye!"

topics.title: Linking words: and, but, because, if
topics.summary: The little words that turn short sentences into real speech.

blocks.arabic: كنت بدّي اجي بس ما قدرت
blocks.english: I wanted to come but I couldn't
I didn't come because I was sick
When I arrived, she was asleep
I think (that) it's going to rain

blocks.text: "bas" = but ("7elo bas ghali": nice but expensive), only ("bas wa7ad": only one) and enough/stop ("bas!").

topics.title: Time: today, tomorrow, what time is it?
topics.summary: Days, parts of the day, telling the time and how often.

head: Latin
Arabic
English
rows: a long time ago; in the old days

blocks.text: sob7 / el sob7 (morning), ba3d el dohr (afternoon), el masa (evening), el leil (night), el dohr (noon). "el sob7" + "bukra" = "bukra el sob7" (tomorrow morning).
"addeish el se3a?" Answer: el se3a + number. Add w (and) for minutes past, illa (minus) for minutes to. robe3 = quarter, nos = half, tilt = twenty minutes.
kel yom (every day), kel jem3a (every week), marra bel jem3a (once a week), dayman (always), ma3 el wa2t (with time), ba3d (still/yet), ba3d ma (not yet: "ba3d ma akalt" = I haven't eaten yet).
"hala2" (now) can mean in five minutes or in an hour. "nshalla" on a plan means "I hope so", not "yes". Ask "akid?" (sure?) if you need a promise.

topics.title: How Lebanese verbs work
topics.summary: One table that explains every tense on the Verbs pages.

blocks.text: Every verb has a **past** form and a **present** form. Everything else is built from the present.

sections.h: The prefixes of the "every day" form

blocks.text: Notice that "you (man)" and "she" are the same: btekteb. The context tells them apart.
"me, you, him" go on the end of the verb with the same endings as "my, your, his" (with -ne for "me").
Learn verbs in pairs: past "he" form + present "I" form (katab / bekteb, akal / bekol). Those two give you everything.

topics.title: Commands and "don't!"
topics.summary: Telling someone to do something, or not to, politely.

blocks.text: There are three forms: to a man, to a woman, to a group. The woman form ends in -e, the group in -o.
Use **ma** + the "you" form of the present without b-: btrou7 → ma trou7 (don't go).
Add **please** (yes, the English word), **iza bitred** (if you like, to a man; "iza btride" to a woman), **min fadlak** (more formal) or start with **fik…?** (can you…?).

blocks.english: Wait a moment, please (to a man)
Could you close the door? (to a man)
Do me a favour / please (to a man)

blocks.text: "tfaddal" (here you go / come in / help yourself), "khalas" (stop, done), "yalla" (come on, let's go), "shouf" (look), "2ol" (say: "2ol mar7aba" = say hello), "dakhlak" (please, I beg you).

topics.title: Call and response: what to say back
topics.summary: Lebanese conversations run on set phrases with set answers. Learn them in pairs.

blocks.text: For many phrases there's one right answer, like "bless you" in English. Answer "shukran" to everything and people will understand, but give the right reply and you'll sound like you grew up there.

head: They say
You answer
When
rows: after a haircut or a shower
well done, may God give you strength
condolences: may God have mercy on him

blocks.english: morning of light (reply to good morning)
on your heart (reply to sa7tein, to a man)
God keep you safe (reply to 3a salemtak, to a man)
and your hands (reply to yeslamo ideik)
God give you health (reply to ya3tik el 3afye)
may God have mercy on your dead too

blocks.text: Endings change with who you talk to: "3a albak" (man), "3a albik" (woman), "3a albkon" (group). If in doubt, use the group form for elders; it's warm and polite.
Say "ya3tik el 3afye" to anyone working: the shopkeeper, the taxi driver, the man fixing your generator. It's thanks and respect in one.

quiz.q: Someone says "sabe7 el kheir". You say…
You thank someone for a meal they cooked:

topics.title: Words you'll hear 100 times a day
topics.summary: yalla, khalas, ya3ne, walla, ma3leish, yi! and friends.

head: Latin
Arabic
What it really means
rows: come on, let's go, hurry; also "ok, bye"
I mean, so, kind of, "um" while thinking
so what? / what does it mean?

blocks.text: "bteje bukra?" "nshalla." This is "I hope so", not "yes". For a real yes you'll hear "akid" or "akid nshalla".
Shopkeepers, taxi drivers and grandmothers all say 7abibi. It's warm, not flirting. Men say it to men all the time.
"yalla bye" is a full Lebanese goodbye. So is "yalla, bye, ciao, bonne journée".

quiz.q: "nshalla" in answer to "Will you come tomorrow?" usually means…

topics.title: French and English in Lebanese
topics.summary: Why you'll hear "hi, kifak, ça va?" and how to join in.

blocks.text: Most Lebanese learn Arabic, French and English at school, and mix them freely. "hi kifak ça va" is a real greeting. You can use English words too: it's normal, not a failure.

blocks.english: Hi, how are you, all good?

blocks.text: Foreign words take Arabic endings: "cancelna" (we cancelled), "btesharje?" (do you charge it?), "fiye a3mol park hon?" (can I park here?).
Use Arabic words when you know them: people notice and smile. But don't stop the conversation hunting for a word. Say it in English and carry on.

quiz.q: Mixing English words into Lebanese is…

topics.title: Manners: visits, food, coffee, respect
topics.summary: What people expect when you visit, eat, greet and talk to elders.

blocks.text: Shake hands with everyone when you arrive and leave, and ask how they are. Friends of the same sex often kiss on the cheek, usually three times (right, left, right). Some religious people don't shake hands with the other sex: wait to see if a hand is offered.
Ask about the family: "kif el 3ayle?" (How's the family?), "kif el wled?" (How are the kids?).

Bring something: sweets, fruit or flowers. Take your shoes off if the hosts do. You'll be offered coffee, juice, fruit and sweets. Saying no once is polite; they'll insist; it's fine to accept the second time.

blocks.english: I don't want to trouble you
What are you saying! (it's no trouble)

blocks.text: Wait for the host to say "tfaddalo" or "sa7tein". You'll be served more than you can eat; leaving a little on the plate tells the host you're full. Praise the food, especially to the cook: "yeslamo ideiki" (bless your hands, to a woman).

blocks.english: I'm full, thanks, it was delicious
Bless your hands (to the woman who cooked)

blocks.text: Turkish-style coffee ("ahwe") is served in small cups. "sada" (no sugar), "wasat" (medium), "7elwe" (sweet). At a funeral it's served bitter. Coffee at the end of a visit often means the visit is ending.

Call older men "3ammo" (uncle) and older women "tante" or "khalto" (auntie), even strangers. Grandparents are "jeddo" and "teta". People are often called by their eldest child's name: "Abu Karim" (Karim's father), "Emm Karim" (Karim's mother).
Religion, politics and the war are sensitive. Listen more than you talk. Money is often discussed openly (rent, salaries, prices), so don't be surprised if someone asks what you pay.
If you're invited "ta3a la 3enna", it's often real. Ask "akid?" and set a day.

quiz.q: Your host insists you have a second plate. You…
You call an older woman you don't know…

topics.title: Phrases with God in them
topics.summary: You'll hear "allah" many times a day from people of every faith. Here's what it means.

blocks.text: Lebanon has many religions, and "allah" phrases are used by Christians and Muslims alike. Using them doesn't say anything about your own beliefs; it's simply polite Lebanese.

head: Latin
Arabic
Meaning
When
rows: praising a child, a house, a success
sympathy for someone busy or struggling

blocks.english: How are you? Fine, thank God

blocks.text: If you praise a baby, a car or a new house, add "mashalla". Praise without it can sound like envy to some people.

quiz.q: Someone shows you their baby. You say…
Are these phrases only for Muslims?

topics.title: Lebanese vs. Standard Arabic
topics.summary: What changes between what people speak and what you hear on the news.

blocks.text: Every Arab country has its own spoken Arabic. Next to it there's **Standard Arabic** (fus7a): the language of the news, books, the Quran and official signs. Nobody speaks fus7a at home. Kifak teaches spoken Lebanese, which is what you need for life in Lebanon.
The letter ق (q) is usually said as 2 in the city: "2alb" (heart), "2ahwe" (coffee). Villagers in some areas keep the q. ث (th) becomes t or s, ذ (dh) becomes d or z.

sections.h: Will Lebanese help with other countries?

blocks.text: Yes. Syrians, Palestinians and Jordanians speak something close to Lebanese (together called "Levantine"), and they'll understand you easily. Egyptians and Gulf Arabs will understand you too, because they watch Lebanese TV and hear Lebanese songs.

quiz.q: Which language do Lebanese speak at home?
The q in "qalb" (heart) is usually said as…

topics.title: Texting in Lebanese
topics.summary: How people write Lebanese on WhatsApp, with the abbreviations.

blocks.text: Most Lebanese text in Latin letters with numbers for the extra sounds, the same system used on this site. Some people write in Arabic script instead. You'll see both.

"kifak", "keefak" and "kefak" are all the same word. "8" for gh, "5" for kh and "9" for heavy s appear in some people's messages. Don't worry about the "right" spelling; read it out loud and it'll make sense.

blocks.english: Did you arrive? (the classic WhatsApp check)
Five minutes and I'll be at yours
I sent you a voice note

blocks.text: Lebanese send a lot of voice notes. They're excellent practice: ask a friend to send you short ones and listen twice.
